title: Must vs Have To vs Should — What's the Real Difference in Competitive English?
excerpt: All three sound like obligation, but exams test the exact line between them. Here's how must, have to, and should actually differ — and where students lose marks mixing them up.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
"Must," "have to," and "should" all get translated the same way in most students' heads — as "obligation." That single mental shortcut is exactly what error-spotting and sentence-improvement questions in SSC CGL and Bank PO are built to catch. These three words don't carry the same weight: one is a personal judgment, one is an external rule, and one is only advice. Textbooks list their meanings side by side and move on, but exams test the boundary between them — and that boundary is where marks quietly disappear.

Quick Answer: "Must" expresses the speaker's own strong opinion or a logical conclusion. "Have to" expresses an obligation imposed by an outside rule, authority, or circumstance. "Should" expresses advice or a mild recommendation, not a firm requirement. All three connect to the base form of the verb, and only "have to" changes form for tense and subject ("has to," "had to").

Table of Contents

  1. Why Must, Have To, and Should Feel Harder Than They Are
  2. Common Mistakes Students Make
  3. The Complete System (Step-by-Step)
  4. A Quick Turnaround Story
  5. Expert Tips From the Classroom
  6. Frequently Asked Questions

Why Must, Have To, and Should Feel Harder Than They Are

In casual speech, these three words get used loosely and nobody notices. In a formal, exam-graded sentence, that looseness is exactly what gets tested. Here's where the confusion usually starts:

  • Students learn all three as "obligation" without learning that the strength of that obligation is different for each one.
  • "Have to" is the only one of the three that changes form ("has to," "had to"), and that grammatical detail gets ignored in favor of memorizing meaning alone.
  • "Should" gets used interchangeably with "must," even though "should" is genuinely optional advice, not a requirement.
  • Negative forms are especially tricky — "must not" (prohibition) and "don't have to" (no obligation) look similar but mean almost opposite things.
  • Students who use these words correctly in daily conversation still hesitate the moment a sentence isolates just one of them for correction.

After years of teaching this exact comparison, one thing is consistent every batch: students already understand these words individually. What trips them up is choosing the right one between two options that both sound grammatically fine — which is precisely the skill sentence-improvement and error-spotting questions are designed to test.

Common Mistakes Students Make

Mistake 1: Treating "must" and "have to" as always identical. Both suggest obligation, but "must" reflects the speaker's personal judgment, while "have to" reflects a rule or requirement coming from outside the speaker.

Mistake 2: Forgetting that "have to" changes form. Unlike "must," which never changes, "have to" becomes "has to" with third-person singular subjects and "had to" in the past.

Mistake 3: Confusing "must not" with "don't have to." "Must not" means something is forbidden. "Don't have to" means something is optional. Mixing these up completely reverses the sentence's meaning.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌ Wrong: She have to submit the form by Friday.
✅ Correct: She has to submit the form by Friday.

❌ Wrong: You must not worry about the exact seating arrangement, it isn't compulsory.
✅ Correct: You don't have to worry about the exact seating arrangement, it isn't compulsory.

❌ Wrong: Candidates should to carry their admit card on exam day.
✅ Correct: Candidates should carry their admit card on exam day.

The Complete System (Step-by-Step)

Instead of treating these as three shades of the same meaning, treat them as three different sources of obligation: "must" comes from the speaker, "have to" comes from an outside rule, and "should" isn't obligation at all — it's advice.

WordSource of ObligationExample
MustSpeaker's own strong opinion or logical conclusionYou must double-check your OMR sheet before submitting.
Have ToExternal rule, requirement, or circumstanceCandidates have to reach the exam center by 9 AM sharp.
ShouldAdvice or recommendation, not a firm ruleYou should revise grammar rules a day before the exam.

Step 1: Ask where the obligation is coming from. If it's the speaker's own conviction, use "must." If it's an external rule, use "have to."

Rule + Example: "I must finish this chapter tonight" (personal resolve) vs. "Students have to wear their ID cards inside the exam hall" (external rule).

Step 2: Remember "have to" is the only one that conjugates. "Have to" becomes "has to" for he/she/it, and "had to" in the past. "Must" and "should" never change form.

Step 3: Treat "should" as advice, not requirement. If a sentence could reasonably be ignored without breaking a rule, "should" is usually the correct choice, not "must."

Rule + Example: "You should attempt the easier questions first" is advice — skipping it isn't wrong, just less strategic. "You must sign the attendance sheet" is a firm requirement.

Step 4: Separate "must not" from "don't have to" carefully. "Must not" forbids an action. "Don't have to" simply removes the obligation — the action is still allowed, just optional.

Step 5: Use "should have" for missed advice in the past, not "must have." "You should have revised this topic" expresses regret over a missed recommendation, while "must have" expresses a logical deduction ("He must have left already").

Step 6: Never combine two of these in a row. "Must should," "have to must" — none of these exist in standard English, however natural they might sound when rushed.

Signal Word / ContextLikely Choice
Rule set by an institution or authorityhave to
Speaker's own strong convictionmust
Friendly advice or suggestionshould
Something forbiddenmust not
Something optional, not requireddon't have to
Regret over a missed recommendationshould have

Step-by-Step Strategy

1

Identify which of the three words is used before judging the rest of the sentence.

2

Ask whether the obligation comes from the speaker or from an outside rule.

3

If it's advice rather than a rule, switch to "should" instead of "must."

4

If "have to" is used, check subject-verb agreement — "has to" or "had to" as needed.

5

For negatives, confirm whether the sentence needs prohibition ("must not") or optionality ("don't have to").

6

Scan for two of these words stacked together — that combination is always incorrect.

A Quick Turnaround Story

A Railway exam aspirant in one of my batches consistently missed sentence-improvement questions involving "must not" and "don't have to," always assuming both meant roughly the same thing. Once we worked through a handful of side-by-side examples — sentences where swapping one for the other completely reversed the meaning — the distinction finally clicked. Her accuracy on this specific question type improved within days, not because the grammar got easier, but because she stopped treating the two as interchangeable and started checking which one the sentence actually needed.

Expert Tips From the Classroom

  • Ask "whose rule is this?" If it's the speaker's own opinion, it's "must." If it's an institution's rule, it's "have to."
  • Treat "should" as removable. If the sentence would still make sense without the obligation, "should" is likely the right word, not "must."
  • Double-check "have to" for subject agreement. It's the only one of the three that changes with person and tense — an easy detail to miss under time pressure.
  • Never assume negatives mirror positives. "Must" and "must not" both express strong statements, but "have to" and "don't have to" point in almost opposite directions.
  • Practice by rewriting the same sentence three ways. Seeing how the meaning shifts with each of the three words builds the instinct faster than memorizing definitions.

The Bottom Line

Must, have to, and should aren't difficult because they're obscure — they're difficult because they all get taught as synonyms for "obligation" when they actually come from three different sources: personal conviction, external rule, and simple advice. Once you start asking where the obligation is coming from before picking a word, this becomes one of the more consistent, predictable scoring areas in the grammar section.

Practice Questions

Q1 (Common Exam Pattern): Find the error: "All candidates must to bring a valid photo ID to the exam center."

Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: "must to bring" → "must bring"

Explanation: Like all modals, "must" connects directly to the base form of the verb, with no "to" in between. The correct sentence is: "All candidates must bring a valid photo ID to the exam center."

Q2 (Common Exam Pattern): Choose the correct option: Employees ______ wear the identity card while inside the office premises, as per company policy.

Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: have to

Explanation: "As per company policy" signals an external rule rather than the speaker's personal opinion, which pairs with "have to" rather than "must."

Q3 (Common Exam Pattern): Find the error: "You must not worry about carrying extra pens, they will be provided at the center."

Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: "must not worry" → "don't have to worry"

Explanation: The sentence describes something optional (pens will be provided), not something forbidden. "Must not" wrongly suggests prohibition, while "don't have to" correctly signals that the action isn't required.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there really a difference between "must" and "have to," or are they the same?

They're related but not identical. "Must" reflects the speaker's own judgment, while "have to" reflects an obligation coming from an outside rule or authority.

Why does "have to" change form when "must" doesn't?

"Have to" behaves like a regular verb phrase and changes with subject and tense ("has to," "had to"), while "must" is a true modal and stays the same in every form.

What's the real difference between "must not" and "don't have to"?

"Must not" means an action is forbidden. "Don't have to" means an action is optional — it's still allowed, just not required.

Is "should" ever as strong as "must"?

No. "Should" always expresses advice or recommendation, while "must" expresses a firm requirement or strong personal conviction. They aren't interchangeable in formal English.

How do I decide between "must" and "have to" quickly during an exam?

Ask whether the obligation comes from the speaker's own opinion (must) or from an external rule, law, or authority (have to). This one question resolves most cases.

title: Participle vs Gerund — How to Tell Them Apart in 10 Seconds
excerpt: Both end in -ing. Both look identical on paper. Yet 'the crying child' and 'the crying of the child' test two completely different grammar rules. Here is the 10-second test that ends the confusion for good.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Two words. Same -ing ending. Completely different jobs. 'The crying child needs help' and 'Crying doesn't solve problems' both use 'crying' — but one is a participle and one is a gerund, and mixing them up is one of the quietest mark-killers in SSC CGL and Bank PO error-spotting. Most students never learn a real test for telling them apart. They just guess by feel — and the exam is built to punish exactly that guess.

Quick Answer: A gerund is an -ing word acting as a noun (Swimming is fun). A participle is an -ing or -ed word acting as an adjective, describing a noun, or helping form a tense (The swimming boy / She is swimming / The broken chair). The 10-second test: try replacing the -ing word with "something" or "it". If the sentence still makes sense, it's a gerund. If it doesn't, it's a participle.

Table of Contents

  1. Why Participle vs Gerund Feels Harder Than It Is
  2. 3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks
  3. The Complete Participle vs Gerund System, Step by Step
  4. A Quick Turnaround Story
  5. Expert Tips From the Classroom
  6. Frequently Asked Questions

Why Participle vs Gerund Feels Harder Than It Is

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic: students don't struggle with the definitions. Almost everyone can say "gerund is a noun, participle is an adjective" on command. What breaks down is applying that definition to an actual exam sentence in real time, especially when the -ing word sits right next to a noun and could plausibly be either.

  • You see an -ing word and label it a gerund automatically, without checking what job it is doing.
  • You confuse a participle describing a noun with a gerund naming an activity, especially in error-spotting options.
  • You forget that participles also form continuous tenses (is running) and passive/perfect structures (broken glass), not just adjectives.
  • You've never used a fixed test — you decide by "feel", and feel fails under exam pressure.
  • I know exactly how that feels — I watched this exact mix-up cost sharp students marks for years before I started teaching one simple substitution test instead of long definitions.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to memorise the theory harder, instead of learning one quick test that settles the question in ten seconds flat.

3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

1. Calling every -ing word a gerund.
Students see "running" and instantly think "noun". But in "The running man crossed the road", running describes man — that's a participle, not a gerund.

2. Treating a participle as if it can take an object like a gerund can.
Gerunds can behave like nouns and take objects in a noun-phrase sense (Reading novels relaxes me). Participles describing a noun cannot be swapped for a plain noun phrase the same way, and forcing that swap creates an unnatural, wrong sentence.

3. Missing participles inside verb tenses altogether.
Students hunt for participles only in adjective positions and completely miss that "is working", "was singing", and "has broken" all contain participles doing tense-forming work, not noun work.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Calling every -ing word a gerund

If the -ing word describes a noun, it is a participle, not a gerund.

Wrong: In "The running man", running is a gerund.

Correct: "Running" here is a present participle describing man.

❌
Mistake 2: Forcing a gerund-style swap onto a participle

A participle describing a noun cannot be turned into an -of phrase like a gerund can.

Wrong: I saw the crying of the child.

Correct: I saw the crying child.

❌
Mistake 3: Missing participles inside verb tenses

"Is working" and "has broken" both contain participles, not gerunds.

Wrong: In "She is working late", working is a gerund.

Correct: "Working" is a present participle completing the continuous tense.

The Complete Participle vs Gerund System, Step by Step

Stop deciding by feel. Run every -ing word through this fixed order, and the answer becomes obvious in seconds.

FormJob in the Sentence10-Second Test
Gerund (-ing)Acts as a noun (subject, object, after preposition)Can you replace it with "something" or "it"?
Present Participle (-ing)Describes a noun, or completes a continuous tenseDoes it sit next to a noun it describes, or follow is/was/am/are/were?
Past Participle (-ed/-en/-t)Describes a noun, or completes perfect/passive tenseDoes it follow has/have/had, or describe a finished state?

Step 1: Find the -ing word and ask what job it is doing. Is it standing in a noun's position, or sitting beside a noun to describe it?

❌ Swimming the boy dived into the pool. (unclear job)
✅ Swimming is good exercise. (gerund — subject, a noun's job)

Step 2: Apply the "something/it" substitution test. If the sentence still makes sense with the -ing word replaced by "something" or "it", it's a gerund.

❌ The crying man annoyed everyone → "The something man annoyed everyone." (fails — so NOT a gerund)
✅ I enjoy reading → "I enjoy something." (test passes — reading is a gerund)

Step 3: Check if the -ing word sits directly beside a noun it describes. If yes, it is almost always a participle, functioning as an adjective.

❌ The sleeping is a child. (sleeping cannot be the naming word here)
✅ The sleeping child did not wake up. (participle describing child)

Step 4: Check if the -ing or -ed word follows a form of "be" or "have". After is/was/am/are/were, an -ing word is a present participle completing a continuous tense. After has/have/had, an -ed/-en word is a past participle completing a perfect tense.

❌ She has broken is a gerund in "She has broken the vase."
✅ She has broken the vase. (past participle completing present perfect tense)

Step 5: Watch for gerunds after prepositions. Any -ing word directly after a preposition (in, at, by, of, without, before, after) is a gerund, never a participle.

❌ He left without saying is a participle.
✅ He left without saying a word. (gerund — noun's job after preposition "without")

Step 6: For introductory -ing phrases at the start of a sentence, check what the phrase describes. This is the classic dangling-modifier trap, and it's always a participle construction, never a gerund one.

❌ Entering the room, the lights went out. (lights did not enter the room)
✅ Entering the room, I switched on the lights. (participle correctly describing "I")

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Ask what job the -ing word does

Noun's job → gerund. Describing a noun → participle.

Example: Swimming is good exercise.

2
Run the something/it test

If it still makes sense, it's a gerund.

Example: I enjoy reading → I enjoy something.

3
Check if it sits beside a noun it describes

That placement almost always signals a participle.

Example: The sleeping child.

4
Check for be/have before it

After be → continuous tense. After have → perfect tense.

Example: She has broken the vase.

5
Watch for gerunds after prepositions

Always a gerund, never a participle.

Example: He left without saying a word.

6
Check introductory -ing phrases for dangling errors

The phrase must describe the very next subject.

Example: Entering the room, I switched on the lights.

A Quick Turnaround Story

One of my SSC CGL students kept losing marks on error-spotting questions built around -ing words — not because she didn't know the definitions, but because she was deciding by ear under time pressure. I gave her only the something/it substitution test and asked her to apply it to every -ing word for a week, nothing else. In her next mock, every gerund-versus-participle question was correct. Nothing else in her preparation changed — just one fixed test replacing a guess. You can do the same — here's how to start.

Expert Tips From the Classroom

  • Never decide by how the sentence sounds. Spoken English blurs gerunds and participles constantly; exam English does not forgive the blur.
  • Run the something/it test first, every time. It settles roughly 80% of questions on its own, before you need any other rule.
  • Treat introductory -ing phrases as a red flag. Always check what noun immediately follows the comma — that's the classic dangling-participle trap.
  • Remember participles do double duty. They describe nouns AND build continuous and perfect tenses — don't only look for them as adjectives.

The Bottom Line

Participle and gerund stop being confusing the moment you stop guessing and start testing. Ask what job the -ing word is doing, run the something/it substitution, and check what it sits beside. That one small habit, repeated consistently, turns this topic from a guessing game into one of your most reliable sources of marks.

Explanation: "Giggling" sits directly beside and describes "students" (Step 3), and fails the something/it test ("the something students" makes no sense), so it is a present participle, not a gerund.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q1. What is the fastest way to tell a gerund from a participle?
Try replacing the -ing word with "something" or "it". If the sentence still makes sense, it is a gerund. If it doesn't, it is a participle.
Q2. Can the same -ing word be both a gerund and a participle in different sentences?
Yes. The same word like "running" can be a gerund (Running is fun) or a participle (The running man) depending entirely on the job it does in that specific sentence.
Q3. Is the -ing word in a continuous tense a gerund or a participle?
It is a present participle. In "She is working", "working" completes the continuous tense — it is not acting as a noun, so it is not a gerund.
Q4. What is a dangling participle and how does it relate to this topic?
A dangling participle is an introductory -ing phrase that ends up describing the wrong noun, because the phrase and the following subject don't match logically, as in "Entering the room, the lights went out."
Q5. Are -ing words after prepositions always gerunds?
Yes. Any -ing word directly following a preposition such as in, at, by, of, without, or before is always a gerund, never a participle.

title: Gerund or Infinitive After Verb? The Complete List for Bank PO Exams
excerpt: Most aspirants lose marks on gerund vs infinitive questions because they memorise long lists instead of learning the patterns examiners actually test. Here is the complete, exam-ready system with the high-frequency verbs and clear decision rules for SSC CGL and Bank PO.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Gerund or infinitive after a verb? This single choice quietly costs SSC CGL and Bank PO aspirants more marks than almost any other grammar point. Not because the forms are difficult, but because textbooks give long memorisation lists instead of the clear patterns that examiners actually test. Once you see the system behind the lists, the confusion disappears.

Quick Answer: After certain verbs we use only the gerund (-ing), after others only the infinitive (to + verb), and after a small group both forms are possible but the meaning changes. Mastering these three groups is enough for almost every exam question.

Table of Contents

  1. Why Gerund vs Infinitive Feels Harder Than It Is
  2. 3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks
  3. The Complete Gerund vs Infinitive System, Step by Step
  4. A Quick Turnaround Story
  5. Expert Tips From the Classroom
  6. Frequently Asked Questions

Why Gerund vs Infinitive Feels Harder Than It Is

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic: students can recite “enjoy takes gerund” and “want takes infinitive”, yet they still choose the wrong form when the sentence looks slightly different or when a verb can take both. The real problem is not memory — it is the lack of a clear decision order.

  • You know many verbs but freeze when you meet a new one in the exam.
  • You mix up the verbs that change meaning with gerund and infinitive.
  • You rely on what “sounds right” in spoken Indian English, which is often wrong in written exams.
  • You have never grouped the verbs into the three practical categories examiners use.
  • I know exactly how that feels — I watched this confusion cost students marks for 22 years before I started teaching the forms as three clear groups instead of one long list.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to memorise every verb separately instead of learning the three patterns that cover almost every question.

3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

1. Using infinitive after gerund-only verbs.
Verbs such as enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep, practise and suggest are followed only by the gerund. Adding “to” is one of the most common errors in Bank PO papers.

2. Using gerund after infinitive-only verbs.
Verbs such as want, decide, hope, plan, refuse, learn and promise take only the infinitive. Students often put -ing out of habit.

3. Ignoring the meaning change with dual verbs.
Stop, remember, forget, try, regret and go on change meaning depending on the form that follows. Examiners test this distinction every year.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Infinitive after gerund-only verbs

Enjoy, finish, avoid, mind and keep never take the infinitive.

Wrong: She enjoys to read before bed.

Correct: She enjoys reading before bed.

❌
Mistake 2: Gerund after infinitive-only verbs

Want, decide, hope, plan and promise take only the infinitive.

Wrong: He decided applying for the post.

Correct: He decided to apply for the post.

❌
Mistake 3: Ignoring meaning change

Stop + gerund and stop + infinitive mean completely different things.

Wrong: He stopped to smoke (when you mean he quit).

Correct: He stopped smoking (he quit the habit).

The Complete Gerund vs Infinitive System, Step by Step

Treat the choice as three clear groups instead of one long list. Once the groups are in your head, most exam questions become straightforward.

GroupForm RequiredCommon Verbs
Gerund only-ingenjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep, practise, suggest, consider, delay, miss
Infinitive onlyto + verbwant, decide, hope, plan, refuse, learn, promise, agree, afford, manage
Both (meaning changes)gerund or infinitivestop, remember, forget, try, regret, go on

Step 1: Identify whether the verb belongs to the gerund-only group. If it does, never use the infinitive.

❌ She avoids to speak in public.
✅ She avoids speaking in public. (avoid takes only gerund)

Step 2: Check for the infinitive-only group. Want, decide, hope, plan and similar verbs are followed only by to + verb.

❌ They hope getting good marks.
✅ They hope to get good marks. (hope takes only infinitive)

Step 3: Master the dual verbs that change meaning. These are the highest-value questions in the exam.

❌ I remember to lock the door (when you mean a past memory).
✅ I remember locking the door. (memory of a past action)

Step 4: Learn the fixed phrases that always take gerund. look forward to, be used to, object to, prefer + -ing, feel like + -ing.

Step 5: Use infinitive of purpose when the sentence shows why someone does something.

❌ He went to the market for buying vegetables.
✅ He went to the market to buy vegetables. (purpose)

Step 6: Practise the high-frequency pairs that appear in almost every paper.

Q1. Which verbs are always followed by a gerund?
Common gerund-only verbs are enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep, practise, suggest, consider, delay, miss and look forward to.
Q2. Which verbs are always followed by an infinitive?

Q3. Do some verbs take both gerund and infinitive?

Q4. Is “to” always part of the infinitive?

title: Gerunds vs Infinitives vs Participles — Clear Rules for SSC CGL & Bank PO
excerpt: Most students mix gerunds, infinitives and participles because textbooks treat them as three separate lists. This post shows the exact decision system that stops the confusion and helps you pick the right form under exam pressure.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Three forms. One verb. Endless confusion. Gerunds, infinitives and participles quietly cost SSC CGL and Bank PO aspirants marks every year because most students learn them as three separate lists instead of one clear decision system. Once you see which form the sentence actually needs, the guessing stops.

Quick Answer: A gerund is the -ing form used as a noun (Swimming is good). An infinitive is to + base verb used as noun, adjective or adverb (I want to swim). A participle is the -ing or -ed form used as an adjective or to form continuous/perfect tenses (The swimming boy / The broken chair).

Table of Contents

  1. Why Gerunds, Infinitives and Participles Feel Harder Than They Are
  2. 3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks
  3. The Complete Decision System, Step by Step
  4. A Quick Turnaround Story
  5. Expert Tips From the Classroom
  6. Frequently Asked Questions

Why Gerunds, Infinitives and Participles Feel Harder Than They Are

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic: students do not struggle with the names. Almost everyone can say "gerund ends with -ing". What breaks down is choosing the right form when the sentence gives no clear signal, or when two forms look possible.

  • You know the definitions but freeze when a verb can take both gerund and infinitive with different meanings.
  • You use "to + verb" everywhere because it feels safer, even when the gerund is required.
  • You confuse the present participle (adjective or continuous tense) with the gerund (noun).
  • You have never seen one simple decision order that works for almost every exam question.
  • I know exactly how that feels — I watched this same mix-up cost students marks for years before I started teaching the forms as one decision tree instead of three lists.

But here's what most people get wrong: they try to memorise long lists of verbs that take gerunds or infinitives, instead of learning the purpose each form serves in the sentence.

3 Mistakes That Cost the Most Marks

1. Using infinitive after verbs that only take gerunds.
Verbs like enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep and practise are followed by the gerund, not the infinitive. Students often add "to" out of habit and lose easy marks.

2. Treating every -ing word as a gerund.
The -ing form can be a gerund (noun) or a present participle (adjective or part of continuous tense). Mixing the two leads to wrong sentence correction answers.

3. Ignoring meaning change with verbs that take both forms.
Verbs like stop, remember, forget and try change meaning depending on whether a gerund or infinitive follows. Examiners love these traps.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Infinitive after gerund-only verbs

Enjoy, finish, avoid, mind and keep take only the gerund.

Wrong: She enjoys to read novels.

Correct: She enjoys reading novels.

❌
Mistake 2: Calling every -ing form a gerund

If the -ing word describes a noun, it is a participle, not a gerund.

Wrong: The running man is a gerund.

Correct: The running man — "running" is a present participle.

❌
Mistake 3: Ignoring meaning change

Stop + gerund and stop + infinitive mean different things.

Wrong: He stopped to smoke (when you mean he quit the habit).

Correct: He stopped smoking (he quit the habit).

The Complete Decision System, Step by Step

Stop memorising long lists. Use this fixed order every time you see a verb form choice in an exam question.

FormMain JobQuick Test
Gerund (-ing)Acts as a nounCan I replace it with "something"?
Infinitive (to + verb)Noun, adjective or adverbDoes it show purpose, intention or result?
Present Participle (-ing)Adjective or continuous tenseDoes it describe a noun or form a tense?
Past Participle (-ed/-en)Adjective or perfect/passiveDoes it describe a finished state?

Step 1: Ask what job the word is doing in the sentence. If it is the subject or object, you almost always need a gerund.

❌ To swim is good for health.
✅ Swimming is good for health. (subject of the sentence needs a gerund)

Step 2: Check the verb that comes before the form. Some verbs take only gerunds, some take only infinitives, and a few take both with a meaning change.

❌ She finished to write the letter.
✅ She finished writing the letter. (finish takes only gerund)

Step 3: Watch the meaning-change verbs. Stop, remember, forget, try, regret and go on change meaning with gerund vs infinitive. Learn the difference once and the trap disappears.

Step 4: Separate participle from gerund by asking one question. Is the -ing word naming an activity (gerund) or describing a noun (participle)?

❌ I saw the crying of the child. (wrong use)
✅ I saw the crying child. (participle describing child)

Step 5: Use infinitive of purpose when the sentence shows why someone does something. "I went to the market to buy vegetables" is purpose, so infinitive is correct.

Step 6: Practise the high-frequency pairs that appear in almost every paper. enjoy + gerund, want + infinitive, stop + gerund/infinitive, remember + gerund/infinitive, look forward to + gerund.

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Ask what job the word does

Subject or object → gerund. Purpose → infinitive.

Example: Swimming keeps me fit.

2
Check the verb before the form

Enjoy, finish, avoid → gerund only.

Example: She avoided meeting him.

3
Learn the meaning-change list

Stop, remember, forget, try change meaning with the form.

4
Separate participle from gerund

Describes a noun → participle. Names an activity → gerund.

Example: the sleeping child (participle)

5
Use infinitive for purpose

When the sentence answers "why", choose the infinitive.

6
Drill the high-frequency pairs

look forward to + gerund, want + infinitive, keep + gerund.

A Quick Turnaround Story

One of my Bank PO students kept choosing the infinitive in almost every question. She said "to + verb" felt safer. We spent three days only on the decision order: first ask the job of the word, then check the verb before it, then check for meaning change. In the next mock she got every gerund-infinitive question right. The only thing that changed was the order she used to look at the sentence. You can do the same — here's how to start.

Expert Tips From the Classroom

  • Always ask "What job is this word doing?" first. Subject or object almost always needs a gerund.
  • Make a small personal list of the ten most common gerund-only verbs. Enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep, practise, delay, consider, suggest, miss.
  • Treat stop, remember, forget and try as special cases. Write one example for each meaning and revise them before every mock.
  • Never decide by sound. Spoken English often mixes the forms; exam English follows the rules strictly.

The Bottom Line

Gerunds, infinitives and participles stop being confusing the moment you stop treating them as three separate lists and start using one decision order: job of the word, verb before it, meaning change, then participle check. Master that sequence and this topic becomes a steady source of marks.

Q2 (Bank PO Exam Pattern): He stopped _____ (smoke) last year and now feels much better.

Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: smoking

Explanation: "Stopped smoking" means he quit the habit. "Stopped to smoke" would mean he paused another activity in order to smoke (Mistake 3 and Step 3).

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q1. What is the main difference between a gerund and a present participle?
A gerund acts as a noun (Swimming is fun). A present participle acts as an adjective or helps form continuous tenses (the swimming boy / He is swimming).
Q2. Which verbs are always followed by a gerund?
Common ones are enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, keep, practise, delay, consider, suggest, miss, and look forward to.
Q3. Can the same verb take both gerund and infinitive?
Yes. Verbs like stop, remember, forget, try and regret take both forms but the meaning changes. You must learn both meanings.
Q4. Is "to" always part of the infinitive?
In most exam questions yes, but after certain verbs (make, let, help, modal verbs) we use the bare infinitive without "to".
Q5. How should I practise this topic for SSC CGL and Bank PO?
Focus on error-spotting and sentence-improvement questions that mix the three forms. Practise the meaning-change verbs every day for one week.

title: How to Identify the Correct Tense in Error Spotting Questions — Step-by-Step Method That Saves Marks
excerpt: Most aspirants lose easy marks in error spotting because they guess the tense instead of checking time markers and verb forms. This post gives you a clear 6-step classroom method so you can spot the right tense in under 30 seconds every time.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Nearly 40% of error-spotting mistakes in competitive exams come from tense confusion alone. One wrong verb form can cost you a full mark, and the examiner never explains why. This post shifts your thinking from “which tense sounds right?” to a fixed checking order that works every time.

Quick Answer: To identify the correct tense in error spotting, first locate the time marker (yesterday, since, already, while), then check whether the action is completed, ongoing, or habitual, and finally match the exact verb form. Ignore what “sounds natural” and follow the time-signal + form pair.

Table of Contents

  1. The Problem
  2. Common Mistakes
  3. The Solution
  4. A Quick Turnaround Story
  5. Expert Tips From the Classroom
  6. The Bottom Line
  7. Frequently Asked Questions

The Real Reason Tense Errors Keep Catching You

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic:

  • You read the sentence and pick the tense that “feels correct” instead of checking the time words.
  • You mix present perfect and simple past because both talk about past actions.
  • You forget that “since” and “for” force present perfect, while “ago” forces simple past.
  • You change a correct verb because the rest of the sentence looks complicated.
  • I know exactly how that feels — you walk out of the exam thinking “I should have got that one right.”

But here's what most people get wrong: they treat tense as a memory topic. It is not. It is a matching game between time signals and verb forms.

Three Mistakes That Cost Marks Every Year

1. Ignoring the time marker.
Students focus on the main verb and forget the small words that decide the tense. “Yesterday”, “last week”, “ago”, “since”, “already” are not decoration — they are instructions.

2. Confusing completed action with ongoing action.
Simple past shows a finished action. Present perfect shows a past action that still connects to now. Mixing them is the single biggest source of wrong answers.

3. Changing the correct form because of subject-verb agreement noise.
When the sentence is long, students start fixing number agreement and accidentally change a correct tense. The two errors are separate.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Ignoring the time marker

You look only at the verb and miss “yesterday” or “since”.

Wrong: She has gone to Mumbai yesterday.

Correct: She went to Mumbai yesterday.

❌
Mistake 2: Mixing simple past and present perfect

Both talk about past, but one needs a finished time and the other does not.

Wrong: I finished my work just now.

Correct: I have just finished my work.

❌
Mistake 3: Changing a correct tense while fixing agreement

Long sentences make you over-edit.

Wrong: The boys who lives next door has left.

Correct: The boys who live next door have left.

ebookcharm — English Grammar Made Exam-Ready

The Classroom Method That Works in 30 Seconds

Stop guessing. Follow this fixed order every time you see a tense error. The order itself prevents most mistakes.

Time SignalUsual TenseExample Form
yesterday / last week / agoSimple Pastwent, finished, saw
since / for / already / just / yetPresent Perfecthas gone, have finished
now / at present / currentlyPresent Continuousis working, are studying
while / when (two actions)Past Continuous + Simple Pastwas reading when the phone rang
every day / always / usuallySimple Presentgoes, works, studies

Step 1: Underline every time word. Circle “yesterday”, “since”, “already”, “while”, “ago”. These words decide the tense before you even look at the verb.

Step 2: Ask — is the action finished or still connected to now? Finished + past time marker = simple past. Connected to present = present perfect.

❌ She has left the office an hour ago.
✅ She left the office an hour ago. (ago forces simple past)

Step 3: Check if two actions happen at the same time. One long action + one short action usually needs past continuous + simple past.

Step 4: Look at the verb form itself. Has/have + V3 = present perfect. Was/were + V-ing = past continuous. Simple past is just V2.

Step 5: Confirm subject-verb agreement only after the tense is fixed. Never change a correct tense while fixing “is/are” or “has/have”.

Step 6: Read the full sentence once with your chosen form. If the time marker and the verb form match, you are done. Do not overthink.

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Underline time markers first

Find yesterday, since, ago, already, while before touching the verb.

2
Decide finished vs connected to now

Finished + past time = simple past. Link to present = present perfect.

3
Check simultaneous actions

While/when often needs past continuous + simple past pair.

4
Match the exact verb form

V2 for simple past, has/have + V3 for present perfect, was/were + V-ing for continuous.

5
Fix agreement only after tense is set

Never change a correct tense while correcting is/are or has/have.

A Quick Turnaround Story

Ravi was stuck at 18–20 marks in English for months. His error-spotting score was always the weakest. He kept changing correct verbs because the sentences felt long. One evening I made him follow only the six steps above on twenty old questions. He stopped looking for “what sounds right” and started underlining time markers first. In the next mock he scored 26. The difference was not new grammar knowledge — it was a fixed checking order. You can do the same — here's how to start.

Expert Tips From the Classroom

  • Never start with the verb. Always start with the time word. The verb form is the last thing you decide.
  • Treat “ago” and “since” as opposite signals. “Ago” kills present perfect. “Since” demands it.
  • When two actions share the same time, one is usually continuous. The longer background action takes “was/were + V-ing”.
  • If you change more than one word, you are probably over-editing. Most tense errors need only one form change.

The Bottom Line

Tense errors in error spotting are not about memory. They are about matching a clear time signal to the correct verb form. Follow the six steps, ignore what “sounds natural”, and the marks start coming back.

Practice Questions (Exam Pattern Drills)

Q1 (SSC CGL Exam Pattern): She has been working in this office since five years.

Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: She has been working in this office for five years.

Explanation: “Since” needs a point of time (2019, Monday). “For” is used with a period of time (five years). This is covered in Step 1 and Step 2 — time marker decides the preposition and confirms present perfect continuous.

Q2 (Bank PO Exam Pattern): When I reached the station, the train already left.

Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: When I reached the station, the train had already left.

Explanation: Two past actions — the earlier one takes past perfect. “Already” also signals completion before another past moment. This matches Step 3 and Mistake 2 correction.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q1. How do I quickly decide between simple past and present perfect?
Look for a finished time word. If you see “yesterday”, “last year”, “ago” — use simple past. If the action still connects to now or has no finished time — use present perfect.
Q2. Can “just” and “already” be used with simple past?
In exam English, “just” and “already” almost always take present perfect. Stick to that rule for error spotting.
Q3. What if there is no clear time marker in the sentence?
Check the meaning. Is the action finished and over, or does it still matter now? Also look at other verbs in the sentence for sequence clues.
Q4. Is past perfect still asked in recent exams?
Yes. Questions with two past actions (“when I reached… the train…”) still appear regularly. Learn the “earlier action = had + V3” rule.
Q5. Should I change the tense if the sentence only has a subject-verb agreement error?
No. Fix only the agreement. Changing a correct tense is a common over-editing mistake (see Mistake 3).

title: Question Tags: Zero Errors — The Complete SSC CGL & Bank PO Guide [2026]
excerpt: You know the polarity rule. You still lose marks. Here is the complete, exam-tested system for question tags — every fixed exception, every hidden trap, and the 186 rules serious aspirants actually need.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
You Answer 8 Out of 10 Right. The Exam Still Beats You.

Eight out of ten SSC CGL aspirants can recite the basic question tag rule in their sleep. Positive statement, negative tag. Negative statement, positive tag. Then the exam hands them 'Nobody objected, did he?' or 'I am late, isn't I?' and the confidence disappears in half a second. Question tags don't fail you because you don't know the rule — they fail you because the exam is built entirely around the five exceptions nobody drills properly.

Quick Answer: A question tag repeats the main clause's auxiliary verb, reverses its polarity, and matches the subject with the correct pronoun. Five fixed forms — aren't I, shall we, didn't (for used to), isn't/aren't there, and they (for nobody/everybody/someone) — account for the majority of tag errors in SSC CGL and Bank PO exams. Mastering these five plus the polarity rule closes almost every gap.

Table of Contents

  1. Why Question Tags Keep Beating Strong Students
  2. 5 Mistakes That Repeat Every Single Year
  3. The 7-Step System for a Perfect Tag Every Time
  4. How Rahul Went From 3 Wrong to Zero Wrong
  5. Expert Tips From 15+ Years of Coaching
  6. Frequently Asked Questions

Why Question Tags Keep Beating Strong Students

Here's the part nobody explains properly: question tags aren't tested to check if you know the rule. They're tested to check if you can apply the rule under pressure, inside a sentence built specifically to hide the trap. Every wrong answer choice in an SSC or Bank PO tag question is designed around one specific blind spot.

  • You apply the polarity rule correctly, but miss that 'hardly', 'never', or 'seldom' already made the sentence negative — so you flip the tag the wrong way.
  • You freeze on 'I am' and default to 'amn't I' or 'isn't I', both of which are always wrong in standard exam English.
